item.content:encoded:
lurker usually; I just wanted to say that I loved this deeply and felt genuinely unsettled/shaken through the entire thing.

I think what got me is the depictions of trauma and how brutally personal everything is —it's not just "some disaster happening far away", it's something happening to these specific people, it's personal. especially the running theme of trauma and its long, long-lasting impacts in the way people think even after it's over … the parts about how it was his fault or if he could just be better or …

I also really enjoyed the drastic shifts in POV/tone that come through the entire piece, and the multiple perspectives on the entire thing. how some people respond differently than others. obviously francis and his mother's comments are the highlight, the scp's cold and clinical tone works in the context of francis's lack of recovery, and the whole run-on comma-less prose is the same kind of breathless anxiety that would come in moments like that.

I can't speak to the other articles on this site (maybe they're just as effective too) but this, to me, is the standout article of the whole scarlet king thing. it's the only one that got me to care. people talk about how fear is the main component of the ritual, this goes and shows what that actual fear looks like.

not to harp on this debate again, but I really don't give a damn about what qualifies as "an SCP" or not. I've lurked the site since 2014 or whenever the 2000 contest was running, and have seen the "style" of SCPs change. things change, art forms change and evolve, and trying to "preserve" the platonic ideal of an SCP is futile. because there isn't one, and everyone has a different idea.

anyway i know you arent on this website anymore so i guess this is all just for me at this point. if by some chance you read this, I hope you're doing well with your future endeavors

item.content:encoded:
I adore this piece, with the exception of exactly one fact which I truly hate: it's not a tale. I know, I know, this horse has been beaten to death, but the thing is, I'm fascinated, with both Dr. Clef and the Scarlet King. This story could be incredible - hell, it could be its own tale hub, honestly, with how engaging and well written it is. The scenes are painted in such vivid detail, and most importantly they actually have some goddamn weight to them, unlike things like the Broken Masquerade which are too busy making weird, obscure jokes to actually show the true implications of their subject. (Apologies for the callout) This would be one of the best articles on the site, if it was only a tale. But no, it takes up an SCP slot, and I feel like that's actually an active detriment to the piece.

I've felt for a little while now like SCPs are no longer about telling good stories, and instead about flashy formats and crafting their own little universes - the latter of which isn't that bad. I'll give you this, you didn't resort to black highlighter to make your piece unique, you actually stuck to your guns and used the tools you had to write a compelling, interesting article. Plus, you didn't really link any other SCPs - an annoying fad among the SCPs on this site, where people tend to just throw in other SCPs they did/like. The only one you inserted made total sense, in context of the story. I digress, though. Once I got into it, I was hooked - but that's the thing. I almost couldn't get into it, because it was just so radically different from any other SCP on the site. I still feel like if this was a tale, I'd upvote it without hesitation - as it is, though, taking up a SCP slot when it has more potential as a full-on tale hub, I'm going to have to no-vote.

That fact pains me, it really does - but the thing is, this story had so much more potential. You could have easily at the very least submitted it as a series of tales - and if you ask me? You wouldn't have had any trouble making it a new hub. Honestly, the whole deal with Dr. Clef and the Scarlet King is just too maddeningly vague (yes, i know, no canon, yada yada, though I do want to mention briefly - if Clef's assholishness is a result/retort to his cruel treatment by the 05s when he was young, you think he'd grow out of being such a wanker, at least in public, over the course of thirty years. In that regard, I really don't see why someone like him would just be drafted into the foundation, and not just locked up somewhere like literally any other reality bender) and something like this would at least be a great interpretation to build off of. As it is, I just can't bring myself to give it anything more than a "meh", if not because of the SCP formatting, then because of the utter waste of potential.

It's a great article. But it's not an SCP.

item.content:encoded:
+ Show Response

Tales are meant to tell stories in an out-of-universe perspective that's totally detached from the Foundation's universe. SCPs on the other hand are a form of storytelling that exists in the Foundation's universe but are carriers of the story they're trying to tell.

If you want to make a point about what defines an SCP, then I think it would be fair if you cited an official definition, and not one that is your own. Granted, I do think you would be hard-pressed to find a definition that all SCPs on the Wiki follow. Any definition would need to describe all extant SCPs, and not dictate a specific standard, because you can't disqualify articles that already exist. And I'm certain that we don't actually have one that integrates all SCPs into a single, universal classification.

But if we did, what would it look like? Well, I think the following is a good place to start.

SCP articles have two things in common:

(1) It appears on the main list.
(2) It details an anomaly.

Now, as broad and generous as this definition is, it's not perfect; I can't even say with certainty that all current SCP articles have at least those two elements.

For instance, there are plenty of articles on other lists (like -EXs and -Js) that are tagged with "scp", and there's even an SCP that's non-anomalous! There are also plenty of articles that play with the notion of traditional in-universe documents, as you point out (see articles tagged "meta").

This, by definition, is NOT an SCP article. It's a Tale posted under an SCP article's slot, and I'm standing by that.

Based on your definition, I honestly think we could argue that this article does fit. After all, this article does have an in-universe format — seen here.

All of this aside. If you want my opinion, the great deal of content contained in this article is immensely creative, compelling, and well-written, and the article here does an excellent job of highlighting the level of narrative complexity. If this article isn't for you, then that's fine! But you can't invalidate this work just because it chooses not to fit inside arbitrary lines drawn 12 years ago, by people that couldn't have predicted what the SCP Wiki would evolve into.

The reason it's posted in an SCP slot is because it's an SCP.

Just because you can call something an SCP, doesn't mean it has what makes it an SCP.

"SCP" is an entirely arbitrary category involving a format used for telling a story in a particular shared universe. Like any writing rule the format is more of a guideline than anything hard. Breaking the format for dramatic effect is arguably half the point of the format.

I'm not talking about that. I'm talking about the in-universe definitive meaning behind what separates SCPs from Tales. Tales are meant to tell stories in an out-of-universe perspective that's totally detached from the Foundation's universe. SCPs on the other hand are a form of storytelling that exists in the Foundation's universe but are carriers of the story they're trying to tell. My issue with this is that it breaks all those established rules for the sake of trying too hard to be something that it clearly wasn't meant to be.

This particular article isn't any different then tons of other SCP's on the site.

Wrong. The difference between this and other SCP articles is that other articles at least have an excuse to be formatted in such a way that they read like tales. This one has none of that and the amount of people excusing this is frankly absurd and ridiculous.

Using the SCP article format as a skeleton to build up a different story around through other supplementary stories.

I've already explained the difference between an SCP and a Tale. This, by definition, is NOT an SCP article. It's a Tale posted under an SCP article's slot, and I'm standing by that.

After having read this site since I was a kid, this is the one that finally made me give in and make an account, just so I could comment on it.

Where do I begin? The section "Frog in a Boiling Pot" and everything else dealing with Francis and Lilly's relationship are incredible. The depiction of Lilly's abuse and Francis' inner state in response to it is incredibly accurate. His feeling that he owes it to her. His anger at her, his attempts to suppress it and prove to himself that he's the one doing something wrong, his guilt over not loving her anymore.

The section "Pigs (Thirteen Different Ones)" is slightly enraging. Not in a bad way - it's angering because it's effectively written. The insinuations that Francis is lying and untrustworthy and that he's the real abuser as well as the downplaying of the abuse he suffered are sadly very believable. The sentence "We also can’t ignore that B is a murderer who killed A- would we give a murderer rights to his child, or to his wife’s body, or to closure at all?" especially sticks out to me in that regard. Especially since Lilly had spent years trying to make him believe he's a liar.

The way Ichabod is discussed - the person comparing the killing of Type Greens to mousetraps and all - is brilliantly disturbing. It's very interesting to see the desperation involved in the subject, with most people just resigning themselves to Ichabod and putting the question of its morality out of their minds. Same thing with the "narrative destabilisation" aspect of the story - the way it calls into question the ability of not only the typical format of an SCP but also many kinds of narratives to accurately show the full picture is simply brilliant. (don't know how to expand on this but i like Coda's character a lot too)

The section "May 23rd, 1989" is just really perfect. It's very good at showing that a lot of the time, abuse is just exhausting to deal with. The final "tell me the truth" is grating and blunt. What Lilly's doing here isn't a stereotypical, dramatic form of abuse - it's a subtle form of gaslighting, intended not only to make Francis think he really is a liar but to wear him down, deny him dignity, press him slowly until he's incapable of caring enough to deny her attacks.
And the second half complements that really well; the depiction of Clef recovering from the nightmare is really good and the fact that he watches Animal House to calm his nerves is just *chef's kiss*

And "SCP-4231-B Test Notes" is really well-executed. It's honestly really sweet to see Clef asserting himself and maintaining his dignity by refusing to cooperate with questioning in elaborate ways. "Making my arms fuzzy" is an oddly cute line and one of my favourites in the whole piece.

The exploration of how Clef's personality has been shaped by his abuse and resultant PTSD is top-notch. He fucks with people and gives false information because his sense of trust is damaged. He takes on an enigmatic name, prevents his face from being photographed, and buries his past because he wants to separate himself from his old life. His problems with women result from being severely abused and raped by the one woman he trusted most. Assuming that the "Profile" section of his personnel file is written by himself (in the Watsonian sense), it's telling that he refers to himself as "it" and calls himself an "inveterate liar" - he's internalised a sense of worthlessness and is dissociated from a sense of being human. (note that this last bit is relatively uncommon in pure PTSD but is practically a defining feature of C-PTSD, which typically results from the kind of long-term abuse and rape that he had to go through.) It really made me feel for him and empathise with him.

The one thing I didn't like was the "Rituals Chapter 1: End" bit at the very end. I'm intrigued by where this goes next, but it also feels out of place; it detracted slightly from the impact of the piece for me. But aside from that, I really can't find many faults with it.

I've been lurking for eleven years. I've read quite a few mainlisters, quite a few tables. On the one hand, this does earn an automatic downvote for being what is essentially a tale in a mainlist slot.

This expands existing canon into strange and painful territory, but the pain resonates for a reason. This has the feel of a story that wanted to be told, and I prefer having read it to not.

Also, there's a lotta slots. I'm okay with this one being hugely unconventional.

So I upvoted. Thank you for your tremendous effort.

Edit: Something that really strongly resonated with me were the super long, comma heavy, run on sentences. The reason that resonates is because that's exactly what my brain feels like during a panic attack, and it's how I speak during the same. I feel less alone being able to read the perspective of a character that, on some level, feels the way I do.

Holy shit. It's good, very good in my opinion, though I can understand some of the critiques. I, for one, greatly enjoy the presentation for this one. Feels almost like a movie, rather than just an article and the multiple (seemingly irrelevant) view points really help to flesh out the world.

I'm not sure if anyone has really bothered to flesh out the character of Alto Clef this much but it's very appreciated. I love how he is presented and it really helps make him seem more believable as an in-univerese character.

Also, I find the concept of two Type-Greens interacting with each other incredibly fascinating from an analytic standpoint. I have yet to see anything on this site attempt to explain what would happen if two reality benders ended up at odds with each and what that would do to the resulting area.

It's horrifying, thought provoking, and somewhat grounded all at the same time. It never really manages to stray into the fantastical and still keeps itself from being utterly mundane. Upvoted with great enthusiasm.

item.content:encoded: This is a great tale, but I urge you to remember that it's supposed to be an SCP. There is an obvious solution, however; trim this down to Item #: SCP-4231, Document SCP-4231-2-A, Excerpt from the confiscated document "The Curious Case of SCP-4231-B", Pigs (Thirteen Different Ones), SCP-4231-B Test Notes, and thats ‘doctor’ asshole to you (and maybe give more official titles to "pigs" and "doctor"). Have "Item #: SCP-4231 be the main text, have everything else in a collapsible or linked page. As for the more tale-like sections, the once that aren't plausibly files in the Foundation database, post them as tales and put links to them at the appropriate points in the story. It would read more smoothly that way, and it wouldn't offend the people (like me) who think the difference between tale and skip is big and needs to stay that way.

The moment I realized that this was going to deal with the Cornwall incident I sucked in my breath. This was clearly going to deal with some major parts of Foundation lore that have so far not been explored, and even if there is no canon this would set a precedent in dealing with it. However, I must say that it was very well handled. It hit all the major points that previous tales have more or less implied (Type Green incident, summoning a god, Clef's origin) without being a full recap or going into wild speculation. Very impressed, and fairly satisfied with how it deals with the implied event.

I will say though, in regards to the discussion of whether or not this should be an SCP, that this doesn't seem to have any special containment procedures, or an SCP that is focused on. Format Screw, and all that, but it doesn't seem to add anything to the article, for me at least, and since SCPs are usually In-Universe foundation documents they often have explanations for why their format is that why, while this doesn't.
